# Background

We will use an example from the book
`A Practical Handbook for Population Viability Analysis` (Morris et al. 1999).

This example demonstrates possible code and techniques to perform population viability
analysis using population Projection Matrix Models using the example in Box 4.1.

A Projection Matrix Model combines life-history data (transitions between different life
stages) and abundance estimates to project possible future outcomes for a population. This
example uses data on American Oystercatchers.

![American Oystercatcher (CornellLab: All About Birds)](figs/American_Oystercatcher_AAB.jpg)

# Julia packages and environments

Julia uses environments to install and manage different packages that are used in a project.
This is accessed by pressing `]` in the Julia terminal (return using `Ctrl + c`).

<!-- Can also be accessed using `Pkg.*()` e.g. `Pkg.add()` or `Pkg.rm()` -->

Required package names are recorded in the `Project.toml` file. Julia and package versions
are recorded in the `Manifest.toml` file. These are machine-edited files that do not need to
be edited manually.

Package management commands: - `activate` : activate a new environment in the current
folder. This creates `Project.toml` and `Manifest.toml` files to create an environment. -
`instantiate` : setup an environment from existing `*.toml` files. This is used if you clone
a project from GitHub for example. - `add` : Add a package (can include versions or GitHub
repositories). - `rm` : Remove a package from the environment. - `status` : See current
environment status (packages and julia version). - `pin` : Set the version of a package(s)
to be stable. This is useful for reproducibility and ensuring consistent package version
use.

## Example

Use the REPL (terminal) to activate the package manager, and add `DataFrames` package. `]`
-\> `add DataFrames`

Then the package can be loaded in the session.

```{julia}
using DataFrames # `using` is similar to `library` in R.
using Statistics # provides statistical functions such as `median`, `quantile` etc.

# You can also use `import` instead of `using`
```

# Step 1: Stage-structured matrix

The first step of using a Projected Matrix Model is to create a transition matrix between
components of the target population.

- Matrix rows and columns represent stages of the population of interest
- Values represent the rate of transition (annual or other temporal scale) between each
  combination of size classes
- Columns represent the stage transitioning FROM and rows represent the stage transitioning
  TO

To do this in Julia we create an object of type `Matrix{Float64}`.

```{julia}
# This is a square matrix where values represent transitions between population stages
# This matrix is in the format:
#                                   FROM
#                   Juveniles   Sub-adults  Adults
#       Juveniles       0           0           0.054
#   TO: Sub-adults      0.665       0           0
#       Adults          0           0.724       0.95

# There are multiple ways to create this matrix
# Simplest: Creating a matrix of Float64 values directly
ao_stage_matrix = [
    0      0      0.054;
    0.665   0      0;
    0      0.724  0.95
]

# Creating a matrix from DataFrame columns
ao_stages = DataFrame(
    to = ["juveniles", "sub_adults", "adults"], # Vector of strings
    juveniles = [0, 0.665, 0], # Vector of Float64
    sub_adults = [0, 0, 0.724],
    adults = [0.054, 0, 0.95]
)
# From selection of columns
ao_stage_matrix = Matrix(ao_stages[:, [:juveniles, :sub_adults, :adults]])

# From 'inverse' selection of columns
ao_stage_matrix = Matrix(ao_stages[:, Not(:to)])

ao_stage_matrix
```

# Step 2: Initial population conditions

Step 2 is to setup the initial population conditions in a population state vector. This
holds current values for the abundance of each stage (i.e. N~0~).

```{julia}
# Initial population state in the format
#       J  S-A  A
N_0 = [40, 50, 60]
```

# Step 3: Matrix multiplication projection

The third step in projection matrix modelling is to project the population state using
transition values.

```{julia}
N_1 = ao_stage_matrix * N_0
```

# Projection Matrix Modelling

Now we can turn the matrix multiplication into a model function that will project the
population for a determined number of years.

Creating a function in julia uses the `function`, `return`, and `end` keywords.

```{julia}
function project_model(
    initial_conditions::Vector{<:Real},
    transition_parameter_matrix::Matrix{Float64},
    years::Int64
)::Matrix{Float64}
    # Create an empty array to hold the results for the model
    n_components = length(initial_conditions)
    proj_results = fill(NaN, n_components, years + 1)

    # Allocate the initial conditions to the initial year column
    proj_results[:, 1] = initial_conditions
    
    # Now loop through each year and combine the transition matrix with the previous year's population state
    for year in 1:years
        proj_results[:, year + 1] = transition_parameter_matrix * proj_results[:, year]
    end

    return proj_results
end
```

# Visualisation

Now we can project the population model for 100 years and visualise the projections.

```{julia}
projections_100t = project_model(N_0, ao_stage_matrix, 99)
```

There are two main ecosystems for visualisation in julia: Plots.jl and Makie.jl

I will focus on Makie.jl for this session. `Makie.jl` is an ecosystem that contains a
backend package (you do not need to install) and several front-end packages (that you will
install) depending on your use case.

- CairoMakie.jl is great for fast, high resolution, publication quality plotting.
- GLMakie.jl is great for plotting interatively (zoom, navigate) while developing plots.
- Makie.jl also interacts with `AlgebraOfGraphics.jl` which is a plotting package similar to
  `ggplot2` in R.

## Plotting with base Makie.jl for fine-scale control

Using Makie.jl (with CairoMakie or GLMakie frontend) allows more fine-scale control, and
more plot types (e.g. animations, 3D plots) but can take more time to develop compared to
AlgebraOfGraphics.jl.

```{julia}
using CairoMakie

# Basic plotting:
fig = series(projections_100t)

# Finer control plotting:
fig = Figure(size = (650, 450), fontsize=12)
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel="Abundance", ylabel="Timestep")

series!(ax, projections_100t, color=[:red, :green, :blue]) # Adding control of colours
legend_entries = [
    PolyElement(; color=:red),
    PolyElement(; color=:green),
    PolyElement(; color=:blue)
]
Legend(fig[2, 1], legend_entries, ["juveniles", "sub_adults", "adults"]; tell_width=false, tell_height=false, orientation=:horizontal)

fig
```

## Plotting algebraically with AlgebraOfGraphics.jl for speed

AlgebraOfGraphics.jl (AoG) allows you to get quickly get from DataFrame to a figure, similar
to how ggplot2 works, but has fewer plot types available than base Makie.jl. AoG uses
Makie.jl behind the scenes, so all plots can be custom modified using Makie.jl syntax to add
legends, colour bars etc.

```{julia}
# using GLMakie # Would usually be required if not loaded already
using AlgebraOfGraphics

# To work with AlgebraOfGraphics.jl we need a DataFrame, similar to ggplot2 in R
# To do this we transpose the matrix and add column names
projection_df = DataFrame(Matrix(projections_100t'), ["juveniles", "sub_adults", "adults"])
projection_df.timestep = 1:nrow(projection_df)

# Convert this to a long-format `stack` is equivalent to `pivot_longer` (`unstack` is equivalent to `pivot_wider`)
projection_df = stack(projection_df, [:juveniles, :sub_adults, :adults], :timestep; variable_name=:stage, value_name=:abundance)

# Plotting with AlgebraOfGraphics
# mapping() is equivalent to `aes` in ggplot() functions
# visual() determines the type of plot
# draw() renders the output, and applies additional settings e.g. figure sizes, layouts, fontsize etc.
projection_lines = data(projection_df) * mapping(:timestep, :abundance, color=:stage) * visual(Lines)
fig = draw(projection_lines)
```

# Example of stochastic simulation and plotting workflow with multiple dispatch

Transition rates may be affected by stochastic environmental variation, affecting population
projections.

In this example we incorporate stochasticity by drawing our rate values from continuous
distributions. For simplicity, we will use uniform distributions of rate values loosely
based on the values from Morris et al. (1999).

We will only vary the fecundity rates (adult to juvenile transition) and adult survival
rates (adult to adult transition).

The `Distributions.jl` package provides functionality for statistical distributions and
sampling. We use `Dirac()` to just sample a constant value (i.e. keep values from Morris et
al.) and `Uniform(a, b)` to specify a uniform distribution between values `a` and `b`.

We format these distributions in a matrix. We then use Julia *broadcasting*. Broadcasting
runs a function over each element in an array. This functionality uses a `.` before function
brackets and the same as using a `for` loop or `map` function to sample each of the
distributions in our object.

## Creating distributions

```{julia}
using Distributions

# Create a matrix of distributions for our sampling
# This is not the most efficient way to sample matrices since most of the values are constant,
# but here we use it to demonstrate broadcasting

dist_stage_matrix = UnivariateDistribution[
    Dirac(0.0)      Dirac(0.0)      Uniform(0.054 - 0.05, 0.054 + 0.05)
    Dirac(0.665)    Dirac(0.0)      Dirac(0.0)
    Dirac(0.0)      Dirac(0.724)    Uniform(0.95 - 0.05, 0.95 + 0.05)
]

# Formatting the distributions as a matrix ensures that when drawn with rand.(), we keep the matrix format
rand.(dist_stage_matrix)
```

We can now sample values for many different model projections.

## Multiple dispatch

Multiple dispatch is a feature that lets you define multiple methods for a single function
depending on the type of the arguments given. This means that functions can have different
behaviour depending on the type of arguments.

Currently our function `project_model()` has one method, where the
`transition_parameter_matrix` argument is of the type `Matrix{Float64}` (so this will not
work with our distribution matrix).

We can use multiple dispatch to create a second method for this function so that different
behaviour is used when the type of `transition_parameter_matrix` is
`Matrix{UnivariateDistribution}`.

Defining a new method for the function is the same how we defined a function earlier.

```{julia}
function project_model(
    initial_conditions::Vector{<:Real},
    transition_parameter_matrix::Matrix{UnivariateDistribution},
    years::Int64
)::Matrix{Float64}
    # Create an empty array to hold the results for the model
    n_components = length(initial_conditions)
    proj_results = fill(NaN, (n_components, years + 1))

    # Allocate the initial conditions to the initial year column
    proj_results[:, 1] = initial_conditions
    
    # Now loop through each year and combine the transition matrix with the previous year's population state
    for year in 1:years
        proj_results[:, year + 1] = rand.(transition_parameter_matrix) * @view proj_results[:, year]
    end

    return proj_results
end
```

## Simulations

Now we can use this new model method to project many stochastic simulations of our PMM and
visualise the results. We still use `N_0` as our initial population state, and model `99`
years.

```{julia}
# We will run the model for 100,000 simulations
n_stages = length(N_0)
n_sim = 100000
years = 99

# Setup results array
stochastic_results = fill(NaN, n_stages, years + 1, n_sim)

# Use a for loop to perform each simulation.
# This could easily be parallelised using the FLoops.jl package by adding @floop before `for`
for i in 1:n_sim
    stochastic_results[:, :, i] = project_model(N_0, dist_stage_matrix, years)
end

stochastic_results
```

# Plotting

To understand how environmental variation translates to population variation we might plot
individual timeseries. Here we will plot 2,000 out of the 100,000 timeseries for speed.

```{julia}
fig = Figure(size=(650, 450))
ax = Axis(fig[1,1], xlabel="Timestep", ylabel="Abundance")

idx = rand(1:100000, 2000)
colours = Makie.wong_colors()[1:3] # Use the same colour palette as AlgebraOfGraphics.jl

for i in idx
    series!(ax, stochastic_results[:, :, i], color=map(x -> (x, 0.3), colours))
end

# Add the original deterministic projections on top
series!(ax, projections_100t, solid_color=:black)

legend_entries = [
    PolyElement(; color=colours[1]),
    PolyElement(; color=colours[2]),
    PolyElement(; color=colours[3])
]
Legend(
    fig[2, 1], 
    legend_entries, 
    ["juveniles", "sub_adults", "adults"]; 
    tell_width=false, 
    tell_height=false, 
    orientation=:horizontal
)

fig
```
